drills.q: Explain in one sentence why BERT can't be used for autoregressive text generation.
drills.a: Bidirectional attention lets every position see the entire sequence including future tokens, so there's no valid next-token-given-only-the-past distribution to sample from.

drills.q: Name BERT's two pretraining objectives and say which one RoBERTa removed.
drills.a: Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). RoBERTa removed NSP and matched or beat BERT with more data, longer training, and bigger batches.

drills.q: You have a base BERT checkpoint (not fine-tuned) and need sentence embeddings for semantic search. Which pooling strategy, and why?
drills.a: Mean pooling over all token vectors, masking padding. [CLS] pooling is unreliable here because [CLS]'s only pretraining signal was the weak NSP objective, so it was never optimized to summarize sentence meaning.

drills.q: Define bi-encoder and cross-encoder in terms of what can and cannot be precomputed.
drills.a: Bi-encoder: query and document encoded independently, document vectors precomputed offline, O(1)-ish ANN lookup at query time. Cross-encoder: query+document encoded jointly with attention across both, score depends on both together, cannot be precomputed, costs one full forward pass per candidate.

drills.q: Estimate: a cross-encoder reranker takes ~1ms/pair batched on GPU. Running it over a full 10M-document corpus per query would take roughly how long, and what do you do instead?
drills.a: Roughly 10,000 seconds (~2.8 hours) per query — infeasible. Instead run a cheap first-stage retriever (BM25 or bi-encoder ANN) to narrow to ~100-500 candidates, then cross-encode only that shortlist.

drills.q: A teammate says ColBERT is 'basically a cheap cross-encoder.' Correct them.
drills.a: It isn't — ColBERT never jointly encodes query and document. It precomputes per-token document embeddings independently (like a bi-encoder) and only combines query and document at the final MaxSim scoring step, which is what keeps it precomputable and cheap at index time.

drills.q: Your team wants to use a GPT-4-class LLM to classify support tickets into 5 fixed categories at 2M tickets/day. What do you propose instead, and why?
drills.a: A fine-tuned NER/classification encoder. Five fixed labels is bounded-output classification; at 2M/day the cost and latency gap (encoders run roughly 15-250x faster and 20-200x cheaper at equal-or-better accuracy) becomes a real infrastructure decision, not a rounding error.

drills.q: Why can't you cache a cross-encoder's per-document representation the way you cache a bi-encoder's document vector?
drills.a: Joint attention means the document's internal representations at every layer are shaped by the specific query tokens attending into them during that forward pass — there's no query-independent intermediate state to freeze and reuse across different queries.

drills.q: Retrieval accuracy after adding a cross-encoder reranker is still poor. Before assuming the reranker is broken, what do you check first?
drills.a: First-stage recall@N — whether the retriever's shortlist actually contains the relevant documents at all. A reranker can only reorder what's in the shortlist; if recall is bad upstream, perfect reranking still returns wrong results, and the fix is on the first-stage retriever, not the reranker.

drills.q: Explain why ModernBERT's changes (RoPE, Flash Attention, alternating local/global attention) don't change the fundamental encoder-vs-LLM decision, but do change something else. What?
drills.a: They keep the same bidirectional-encoder-plus-MLM recipe, so they don't change when you'd choose an encoder over an LLM in kind. What they change is the ceiling on what encoders can handle well — longer documents (8192 tokens) and higher throughput — strengthening the case for encoders on tasks that used to be borderline due to context-length limits.

drills.q: A classifier fine-tuned with a head on [CLS] performs worse after someone 'simplifies' the code to use mean pooling instead, without retraining. Why did that break it?
drills.a: The classification head's weights were trained specifically against the [CLS] vector's post-fine-tuning representation. Swapping to mean pooling feeds the head a differently-distributed vector it was never trained on, so the learned decision boundary no longer applies — pooling strategy must match how the model was actually trained, not be chosen independently at inference time.
